source_refs.note: Topic 1.7.7, printed pages 13-14, as printed: the trends in electronegativity with Fig 1.8 and the summary Fig. 1.9.

blocks.text: When we move from left to right along the period, the electronegativity increases. This is due to increasing nuclear charge and decreasing size. In the groups, it decreases from top to bottom this is due to the increase in size due to the addition of shells and increasing shielding effect. For example, in the halogen group, the electronegativity value decreases from fluorine (4.0) to iodine (2.5) as shown in a part of the periodic table in Fig 1.8.

blocks.alt: Part of the periodic table with Pauling electronegativity values: H 2.1 on the top arrow; Li 1.0, Be 1.5, B 2.0, C 2.5, N 3.0, O 3.5, F 4.0; Na 0.9, Mg 1.2, Al 1.5, Si 1.8, P 2.1, S 2.5, Cl 3.0; K 0.8, Ca 1.0, Br 2.8; Rb 0.8, Sr 1.0, I 2.5. An arrow across the top and an arrow up the right side are both labelled Electronegativity increases.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.8: Variation of electronegativity in groups and periods (original drawing after the textbook's Fig 1.8).

blocks.text: Normally, metals being on the left side of the periodic table, possess lower electronegativity values than those of non-metals. Hence, metals are electropositive and non-metals are electronegative, relatively.
Figure 1.9 provides a summary of all the variation trends in various physical properties of elements in the periodic table.

blocks.alt: A skeleton periodic table with labelled arrows. Across the top, Ionization energy and Electron affinity point to the right; on the right side, Electron affinity and Ionization energy point up. Atomic radius points down on the left side and from right to left along the bottom. Across the table, Nonmetallic character points up to the right and Metallic character points down to the left.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.9: Trends in various physical properties in the periodic table (original drawing after the textbook's Fig. 1.9).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 1.9 spells 'Electon affinity' and draws a 19-column grid with period 7 cut short; it is drawn above as 'Electron affinity' on the 18-group, 7-period table.
